WBCQ's 500 kW Superstation: Owner Seeks a Lease, or a Buyer, After 9330 kHz Went Silent

By Michael Smith · October 12, 2026 · Updated October 21, 2026 · 6 min read

The 500 kW “Superstation” at WBCQ in Monticello, Maine has been silent on 9330 kHz since January. Now the organization that says it owns the transmitter, World’s Last Chance (WLC) Radio Ministry, has told ShortwaveHQ it wants to lease the station out, or sell it if no tenant comes forward. WLC set no asking price, and the FCC license is not part of the deal.

Updated October 21, 2026: added statements WLC Radio Ministry sent to ShortwaveHQ on October 17, the two accounts of why 9330 kHz went silent, who owns and operates what, and what a lessee would need to know. WBCQ owner Allan Weiner has been asked for comment; this article will be updated if he responds.
At a glance
  • What: a 500 kW Continental Electronics transmitter and a rotatable curtain antenna in Monticello, Maine, last used on 9330 kHz
  • Owner (per WLC): WLC Radio Ministry
  • Operator and FCC licensee (per WLC): Allan Weiner of WBCQ
  • On offer: a lease first; a sale if no lessee appears; liquidation as a last resort (WLC)
  • Price: none set. WLC invites offers.
  • FCC license: not for sale; operating and licensing arrangements would be handled separately
  • WBCQ itself: still on the air on its other shortwave frequencies

What WLC told ShortwaveHQ

In two emails on October 17, 2026, Galal Doss of WLC Radio Ministry laid out the ministry’s position. Before January, he wrote, the Superstation “was neither for sale nor for lease.” That changed, according to WLC, “after the theft of our entire digital treasury in January,” which forced the ministry to “abruptly halt broadcasting.”

WLC first tried to lease the station so it could wait for the funds to be recovered, but Doss said those efforts “yielded no inquiries.” Nearly ten months on, he wrote, the ministry “can no longer afford to maintain the station even in an idle state,” and has begun exploring a sale, or liquidation if no buyer appears.

His second email made the priority clear: “The ministry prefers an outright lease of the superstation.” A lease would buy time and relieve WLC of the cost of an idle facility. A sale is the fallback.

On price, Doss wrote that WLC has “not set a target price” and invites serious parties to make an offer. He added that if the ministry’s funds are restored, WLC will take the station off the market.

Two accounts of why 9330 kHz went silent

SourceWhat they say
WLC Radio Ministry (October 2026)Broadcasting stopped after the theft of its “entire digital treasury” in January.
Hobbyist reports (January 2026)Glenn Hauser’s World of Radio forum relayed that WLC was bankrupt. A message on WLC’s website at the time cited “growing financial challenges,” suspended projects and a request for donations (forum thread).

ShortwaveHQ has not independently verified either account. They are not necessarily in conflict: a theft of funds would explain sudden financial trouble. Both agree on the outcome, which is that WLC stopped paying for and filling 9330 kHz in January.

Who owns what

This is the question Glenn Hauser raised in January, when he asked who now controls the 500 kW unit. WLC’s answer is direct: it says it is the sole owner of the Superstation, while Allan Weiner of WBCQ operates the station and holds the FCC license. That fits the history: the HFUnderground wiki says WLC paid for the 500 kW antenna and Weiner built it (HFUnderground).

WBCQ’s own website has also listed the Monticello Superstation, 9.330 MHz at up to 500 kW with a fully rotatable antenna, as available to lease (wbcq.com, page dated June 9, 2026). Anyone interested should expect to talk with both WLC, as owner, and WBCQ, as operator and licensee. WBCQ has not yet commented to ShortwaveHQ.

What a lessee or buyer should know

  • The license is separate. WLC is not selling the FCC license. Any new operation would need an arrangement with the licensee, or its own licensing.
  • A lease is the preferred route. WLC says it wants a tenant first. Earlier forum reports said WBCQ looks for long-term leases in 12-hour blocks; that is secondhand.
  • The hardware is rare. A 500 kW shortwave transmitter with an antenna that can be aimed at different regions is something very few private broadcasters in the world have.
  • No price is published. WLC asks for offers.
  • How to inquire: contact WLC Radio Ministry through worldslastchance.com and WBCQ through wbcq.com.

WBCQ is still on the air

Only the 9330 kHz Superstation is idle. In the A-26 schedule data, WBCQ The Planet is filed on 7490 kHz and 6160 kHz, and the HFUnderground wiki lists 5130, 6160 and 7490 kHz as active. Check WBCQ’s own program guide before you tune.

What it means for listeners

If a new tenant signs on, 9330 kHz could return with a new program, a new language and a new target area, since the antenna can be rotated. Until then, expect noise or other stations on that channel. Our schedule data still lists 9330 kHz as “WBCQ World’s Last Chance” because the EIBI files lag real life, so treat that listing as out of date; we no longer recommend it in our Tonight guide. The B-26 season starts October 25, and the season change tracker will show whether 9330 kHz is filed again.

No radio handy? Check 9330 kHz on a free WebSDR or KiwiSDR. Our guide to listening to shortwave radio online shows how.

WLC asked ShortwaveHQ to help spread the word to potential lessees. If you run a broadcaster, ministry or program service that could use a high-power shortwave outlet, the contacts are above. Disclosure: ShortwaveHQ has offered to help connect WLC with interested parties. ShortwaveHQ has no financial interest in the station and is not paid by WLC or WBCQ.

Is WBCQ's 500 kW Superstation for sale?

Its owner, WLC Radio Ministry, told ShortwaveHQ in October 2026 that it prefers to lease the Superstation, and will consider a sale if no lessee comes forward. No price has been set; WLC invites offers.

Who owns the WBCQ Superstation?

According to WLC Radio Ministry, WLC is the sole owner, while Allan Weiner of WBCQ operates the station and holds the FCC license. WBCQ has not commented.

Is the FCC license included?

No. WLC says it is not offering the FCC license, so operating and licensing arrangements would have to be handled separately.

Why did 9330 kHz go silent?

WLC says it halted broadcasting after the theft of its digital treasury in January 2026. Hobbyist reports at the time described the ministry as bankrupt. Neither account has been independently verified.

Is WBCQ still on the air?

Yes. Only the 9330 kHz Superstation is idle. WBCQ continues on its other shortwave frequencies, including 7490 and 6160 kHz.
